title: 11. Observability & SRE: Alerting
summary: Alerting is the practice of automatically notifying humans when a system's behavior breaches a threshold or violates a service-level objective, with the goal of bringing human attention to bear on user-visible harm within a…
objectives: What is the difference between symptom-based and cause-based alerting, and why does Google recommend symptom-based?
Explain multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting and why it is the SRE state of the art.
What is alert fatigue, and how do you detect and remediate it?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Alerting is the practice of automatically notifying humans when a system's behavior breaches a threshold or violates a service-level objective, with the goal of bringing human attention to bear on user-visible harm within a time window short enough to limit damage.
An alert is a contract between the system and a human: when the system detects a condition that means a user is being harmed, it will wake someone up. The contract has a moral weight because every alert has a cost — a woken engineer loses sleep, makes worse decisions the next day, and accumulates burnout that ultimately drives them out of the team. A team that pages its on-call engineer 20 times per day is not "highly monitored"; it is abusing its engineers and training them to ignore the channel, which means the one critical alert in those 20 will be missed. The discipline of alerting is therefore the discipline of restraint: page only when a user is being harmed, page exactly once per incident, page the right person, and give them enough context to act in under 60 seconds. Google's SRE book puts this bluntly: "every alert should be actionable, every alert should be novel, every alert should be specific." A team that holds this line operates reliable systems; a team that does not drowns in noise.

The foundational distinction is symptom-based versus cause-based alerting. A symptom is what the user experiences — "checkout is failing for 5% of users." A cause is an underlying condition — "CPU on the database is at 95%." Alerting on causes produces noise because most causes do not produce symptoms (a database at 95% CPU may still serve all queries within SLO) and because causes are correlated (one root cause triggers many cause-alerts simultaneously). Alerting on symptoms produces signal because the symptom is the user-visible harm — if checkout is failing, the user is harmed regardless of which underlying cause produced it. Google's SRE book formalizes this: "alert on symptoms, not causes," and the rule eliminates a huge fraction of alert noise. The cause-based alerts (CPU, memory, queue depth) still belong in dashboards for diagnosis after the symptom alert fires, but they should not page. The exception is when a cause is so reliably correlated with imminent symptom that paging early saves recovery time — for example, a replication lag alert that always precedes a failover — but this must be validated, not assumed.

The second concept is multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting, the SRE state of the art for SLO-based alerts. The intuition is that a service with a 99.9% SLO has a fixed error budget per 28-day window (0.1% of requests, or about 43 minutes of full outage). The team should be paged if the budget is being consumed too quickly, but the threshold depends on the time horizon: a 2% error rate for 1 minute is fine (consumes 0.07% of budget); a 2% error rate for an hour consumes 8% of budget and is a real problem. Multi-window alerting computes the burn rate (errors relative to the budget rate) over multiple windows — typically 1-hour and 5-minute — and pages only when both breach their thresholds. A short-window breach alone is a transient spike that may self-resolve; a long-window breach alone is a slow burn that does not need an immediate page; both together is a sustained problem that needs attention now. Google's SRE workbook specifies the canonical thresholds: page on a 14x burn rate over 1h AND 5m windows (consumes 2% of monthly budget in 1 hour); warn on a 6x burn rate over 6h AND 30m windows. This pattern catches both fast and slow budget consumption while suppressing noise from transient spikes.

The third concept is escalation policies. When an alert fires, the alerting system (PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Alertmanager) routes the page to an on-call engineer. If the engineer does not acknowledge within a configured window (typically 5 minutes), the system escalates — to a secondary on-call, to the team lead, to the engineering manager, eventually to anyone who can break the glass. The escalation policy must balance two goals: getting attention fast enough to limit damage, and not waking up the entire engineering organization for every page. A common pattern is primary on-call (5-minute ack window) → secondary on-call (additional 5 minutes) → team lead (additional 10 minutes) → engineering manager (additional 15 minutes). Each escalation is itself a signal: if escalations are frequent, the primary on-call is overloaded, the runbook is unclear, or the alert is misrouted. PagerDuty, the dominant commercial tool, reports that teams with structured escalation policies have 40% lower mean-time-to-acknowledge than teams with ad-hoc paging.

The fourth concept is alert fatigue, the failure mode where excessive alerts train engineers to ignore the channel. The symptoms are well-documented: pages acknowledged without being read, alerts muted for weeks at a time, on-call engineers dreading their rotation, and attrition concentrated in on-call-heavy roles. The fix is the weekly alert review: every page from the previous week is examined, classified as actionable or not, and either fixed (tune the threshold, fix the underlying condition, silence the alert, route to Slack instead of page) or confirmed as necessary. Teams that hold this review religiously converge to 1–2 pages per day per service, every one of which is actionable. Teams that skip the review drift to 20+ pages per day within months. The 2019 Cloudflare outage, where 4,000+ pages fired in under a minute due to lack of deduplication, is the canonical case study — the team could not even acknowledge pages fast enough, let alone diagnose.

The fifth concept is the alert payload. A good alert includes enough context that the on-call engineer can start diagnosis without a second query: the affected service, the current and threshold values, the time window, a link to the dashboard, a link to the runbook, and a link to the relevant code. A bad alert says "CPU > 80%" with no context, forcing the engineer to spend 5 minutes orienting before they can even begin. The discipline is to treat the alert payload as a mini-runbook: everything the engineer needs to start acting in 60 seconds, in the page itself. Modern alerting systems (PagerDuty, Opsgenie) support rich payloads with clickable links, severity levels, and even auto-generated summaries from LLMs.

The real-world example is Google's own alerting philosophy, documented in the SRE book and refined over 20 years of operating planet-scale systems. Google alerts exclusively on SLO burn rate for user-facing services, with multi-window thresholds tuned per service criticality. The result is that Google's on-call engineers are paged roughly 2–5 times per week per service, despite operating at a scale that would generate thousands of cause-based alerts per day. The lesson is that alerting quality is a function of restraint, not coverage — fewer, better-targeted alerts produce faster recovery than a flood of noise.

The fundamental trade-off in alerting design is sensitivity versus specificity. High sensitivity (page on any anomaly) catches every real incident but also produces many false positives; high specificity (page only on confirmed user harm) minimizes false positives but may delay detection. The SLO burn-rate approach resolves this trade-off by anchoring the alert to user-visible harm: by definition, a breach of the SLO means users are being harmed, so the alert is both sensitive (catches real harm) and specific (does not fire on conditions that do not produce harm). Teams that anchor alerts to SLOs converge to the right balance; teams that anchor alerts to infrastructure thresholds oscillate between too-sensitive and too-specific as they tune thresholds reactively.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Metrics stream] --> B{Alert rules engine}
    B -->|"symptom rule: error_rate > 0.1% for 5m"| C[Page]
    B -->|SLO burn rate 14x in 1h AND 5m| C
    B -->|"cause rule: CPU > 80%"| D[Slack only]
    C --> E[PagerDuty/Opsgenie]
    E --> F{Primary on-call ack in 5m?}
    F -->|yes| G[Engineer investigates]
    F -->|no| H[Escalate to secondary]
    H --> I{Secondary ack in 5m?}
    I -->|no| J[Escalate to team lead]
    G --> K[Runbook + dashboard + trace link in payload]
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
+------------+    metrics    +------------------+
|  Service   | ------------> | Alert rules eng. |
+------------+               +------------------+
                                     |

            symptom rule       SLO burn rate      cause rule
            err>0.1% for 5m    14x in 1h AND 5m   CPU>80%

                  +-----------------+

                  +-----------------+

              primary on-call (ack 5m)?
                  |              |
                 yes             no

                  v              v
            investigate    escalate -> secondary (5m)
                                           |
                                          no
                                           |
                                           v
                                    team lead (10m) -> manager
```

### Walkthrough
1. The metrics stream flows into the alert rules engine, which evaluates multiple rule types: symptom thresholds, SLO burn-rate windows, and cause thresholds.
2. Symptom rules and SLO burn-rate breaches page a human; cause rules route to Slack only (informational, not pageable).
3. PagerDuty (or Opsgenie, Alertmanager) routes the page to the primary on-call engineer with a 5-minute acknowledge window.
4. If the primary acknowledges, they open the runbook link from the alert payload and begin diagnosis; if not, the system escalates to secondary, then team lead, then manager.
5. The escalation chain ensures someone always responds, while the alert payload's runbook and dashboard links let the responder start acting within 60 seconds.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# alerting_engine.py - runnable; SLO burn-rate + symptom alerting with escalation
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum

class Severity(Enum):
    INFO = "info"
    WARNING = "warning"
    CRITICAL = "critical"

@dataclass
class AlertRule:
    name: str
    severity: Severity
    runbook_url: str
    dashboard_url: str

@dataclass
class EscalationPolicy:
    primary: str
    secondary: str
    team_lead: str
    manager: str
    ack_window_seconds: int = 300

    def escalate(self, alert_name: str, ack_received: bool) -> list[str]:
        pages = []
        if not ack_received:
            pages.append(f"PAGE {self.primary}: {alert_name}")
            time.sleep(0.001)  # simulate 5-min wait
            pages.append(f"PAGE {self.secondary}: {alert_name}")
            time.sleep(0.001)
            pages.append(f"PAGE {self.team_lead}: {alert_name}")
            time.sleep(0.001)
            pages.append(f"PAGE {self.manager}: {alert_name}")
        else:
            pages.append(f"PAGE {self.primary}: {alert_name} (acked)")
        return pages

class SLOBurnRateAlert:
    """Multi-window burn-rate alert per Google SRE workbook."""
    def __init__(self, slo: float, service: str, policy: EscalationPolicy):
        self.slo = slo            # e.g. 0.999
        self.service = service
        self.policy = policy
        self.rule = AlertRule(
            name=f"{service}-slo-burn",
            severity=Severity.CRITICAL,
            runbook_url=f"https://runbooks/{service}/slo-burn",
            dashboard_url=f"https://grafana/{service}/slo",
        )

    def evaluate(self, error_rate_long: float, error_rate_short: float,
                 window_long_h: float, window_short_h: float,
                 ack_received: bool = False) -> list[str]:
        # budget_rate = (1 - SLO) per the long window duration
        budget_rate_long = (1 - self.slo) / (window_long_h)   # per hour
        burn_long = error_rate_long / budget_rate_long if budget_rate_long > 0 else 0
        budget_rate_short = (1 - self.slo) / (window_short_h)
        burn_short = error_rate_short / budget_rate_short if budget_rate_short > 0 else 0
        # canonical thresholds: page if burn > 14x in both windows
        if burn_long > 14 and burn_short > 14:
            msg = (f"FIRE: {self.service} SLO burn "
                   f"long={burn_long:.1f}x short={burn_short:.1f}x "
                   f"(threshold 14x). Runbook: {self.rule.runbook_url}")
            return [msg] + self.policy.escalate(self.rule.name, ack_received)
        # warn (Slack only) if burn > 6x in long window
        if burn_long > 6:
            return [f"WARN (Slack): {self.service} burn {burn_long:.1f}x in long window"]
        return [f"OK: {self.service} burn long={burn_long:.1f}x short={burn_short:.1f}x"]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    policy = EscalationPolicy("alice", "bob", "carol", "dan")
    # SLO 99.9% over 28 days, evaluate 1h and 5m windows
    alert = SLOBurnRateAlert(slo=0.999, service="checkout", policy=policy)
    print("--- Scenario 1: normal traffic ---")
    for line in alert.evaluate(error_rate_long=0.0005, error_rate_short=0.001,
                                window_long_h=1, window_short_h=5/60):
        print(line)
    print("\n--- Scenario 2: sustained burn (page) ---")
    for line in alert.evaluate(error_rate_long=0.02, error_rate_short=0.02,
                                window_long_h=1, window_short_h=5/60,
                                ack_received=False):
        print(line)
```
